questions.question: An aircraft with a parabolic polar flies at the same weight at sea level and at 30,000 ft. How do the minimum drag Dmin and its true airspeed Vmd at 30,000 ft compare with sea level?
options: Dmin is the same, and Vmd is higher
Dmin is lower, and Vmd is the same
Dmin is lower, and Vmd is higher
Dmin is the same, and Vmd is the same
questions.explanation: Dmin = W/(L/D)max depends on the weight and the polar only. It occurs at one CL, so its true airspeed rises as 1/√σ; the minimum power rises with altitude.

questions.question: With a parabolic polar and constant C, the best range of a jet is at 1.316 Vmd, where L/D is 0.866 (L/D)max. Why is it there?
options: The product V L/D is highest at 1.316 Vmd
The fuel flow C T is lowest at 1.316 Vmd
The power required D V is lowest at 1.316 Vmd
The parasite drag equals the drag due to lift at 1.316 Vmd
questions.explanation: At constant C the Breguet range is proportional to V L/D, and up to 1.316 Vmd the speed gains more than L/D loses. The fuel flow is lowest at Vmd, which gives the maximum endurance.

questions.question: An invented jet has T/W = 0.25 and (L/D)max = 10, with a thrust that does not change with speed. What is its steepest steady climb, and near which speed is it flown?
options: sin γ = 0.15, near Vmd
sin γ = 0.25, near Vmd
sin γ = 0.15, near VY
sin γ = 0.25, near VY
questions.explanation: sin γmax = T/W − 1/(L/D)max = 0.25 − 0.10 = 0.15, about 8.6°. The angle follows T − D, which is largest at the minimum drag; VY is higher, because the rate is V (T − D)/W.

questions.question: For the Learjet 45 example with a constant thrust, the step integration and the closed form with the average acceleration both give a ground run of 2,246 ft. Why can the two differ when the thrust comes from an engine deck?
options: The thrust varies along the run, and one acceleration at VR/√2 no longer represents it
The closed form leaves out the rolling friction μ (W − L), and the integration keeps it
The closed form ends the run at VR/√2, and the integration continues to VR
The step of 0.25 s is too long once the thrust changes, and the integration loses accuracy
questions.explanation: The closed form takes one acceleration, evaluated at VR/√2, for the whole run to VR, friction included. It matches the integration at constant thrust; a thrust that varies along the run needs T, L, and D at each step.

questions.question: In the braking roll the braking force is μB (W − L). What happens to it when the spoilers open after touchdown?
options: It grows, because less lift leaves more weight on the wheels
It grows, because the spoilers raise the braking friction coefficient μB
It falls, because the spoiler drag takes over part of the braking
It stays the same, because the wheels carry the full weight after touchdown
questions.explanation: Spoilers dump the lift, so W − L and the braking force grow. They also add to the drag D; μB depends on the runway surface.

questions.question: The corner speed V* gives the highest instantaneous turn rate. What limits the turn on each side of it?
options: Below it the stall limits n; above it the structure limits n and ω falls with V
Below it the structure limits n; above it the stall limits n and ω falls with V
Below it the thrust limits n; above it the drag limits n and ω falls with V
Below it the stall limits n; above it n keeps growing with q but ω falls with V
questions.explanation: Along the stall limit n = q CLmax/(W/S) grows with the speed, and the turn rate rises. Above V* the structure holds n at nmax, and ω = g√(n² − 1)/V falls.

questions.section: Specific excess power at load factor
questions.question: At one speed, weight, altitude, and rating, an invented aircraft has Ps = 320 ft/s at 1 g and 200 ft/s at 2 g. What is Ps at 3 g?
options: 0 ft/s
80 ft/s
50 ft/s
questions.explanation: The loss from the 1 g value is proportional to n² − 1: 120 ft/s for n² − 1 = 3, so 320 ft/s for n² − 1 = 8. That leaves Ps = 0: 3 g is the sustained load factor at this speed.

questions.section: The maneuver V-n diagram: Air-to-Air Fighter
questions.question: On the maneuver V-n diagram of the Air-to-Air Fighter, the point at Mach 0.9 and 7.33 g lies on the limit load factor, below the stall line, and above the line of Ps = 0. What is true of a turn at that point?
options: It can be flown, but it loses speed or altitude while it lasts
It cannot be flown, because the thrust cannot balance the drag
It can be held at constant speed and altitude, within the limit load factor
It stalls the wing, because the load factor is above nsus
questions.explanation: The point is within the stall limit and the limit load factor, so the turn can be flown. Above the line of Ps = 0 the drag exceeds the thrust, here Ps = −595 ft/s, and the turn lasts until the speed or the altitude runs out.
